newsitem.title: CHINA: China stocks set to rise with official hands tied.
newsitem.headline: China stocks set to rise with official hands tied.

text.p: China's volatile stock markets look set for further gains over the next few weeks with regulators reluctant to take any serious measures to cool trading down ahead of the Hong Kong handover, analysts said.
"They want to see the market bullish, but not too bullish," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage in Shanghai. "They want slow bulls, not fast bulls."

The regulators are in a dilemma, trapped between a desire to control the strong upward pressure on China stock prices and a need to keep the markets looking positive through the return of Hong Kong to Chinese control at midnight on June 30.
"The time before the handover now is too short, they can't bring in any big measures," said another brokerage analyst.

With Beijing assumed to want the markets to remain on a slow upward track through the crucial 15th Communist Party Congress scheduled for later in the year, many market players sense an opportunity to push up the market relatively free of risk.

On Friday, after the stock markets closed, the securities authorities announced a rise in the stamp tax on stock trading to 0.5 percent from 0.3 percent, but brokers said they saw little impact from the measure.

"The market will drop a bit on Monday and then rebound," said a local brokerage analyst. "Most local investors would not be concerned over this small degree of change. It's just a signal of the government's feelings."
The indices on China's two stock markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen have soared since the beginning of the year despite regular warnings from Beijing about the risks involved in equity investments.

Shanghai's foreign currency B share index closed on Friday at 94.131, up 45 percent since the beginning of the year, while Shenzhen's B share index ended the week at 179.62, up a more modest 22 percent.
The domestic A shares, which make up the bulk of the market capitalisation, have risen even further so far this year -- 60 percent for Shanghai and 50 percent for Shenzhen since January 1.

But market players say they see the rises as being much less speculative than previous surges, and much more linked to fundamental factors, such as the continued healthy growth of the Chinese economy and low inflation.

"Both technical charts and fundamentals support further gains of the B shares in the medium and long run," Guotai Securities analyst Zhang Jun was quoted as saying in Friday's China Securities newspaper.
"China's economy is seen continuing to grow substantially in 1997, which will make listed firms perform better," he said. "I think the B share market is just starting a bull run."
